extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel, publicity directors, business executives, and political campaign managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running propaganda/public-relations campaigns for business and political purposes, covering strategy, media, budgeting, audience analysis, crisis handling, and coordination of appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as complement to advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The new technique of public relations counsel is serving a very useful purpose in business by acting as a complement to legitimate advertisers and advertising in helping to break down unfair exaggerated and overemphatic advertising by reaching the public with the truth through other channels than advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PR to correct or counteract exaggerated competitor claims by reaching audiences via non-advertising channels (e.g., dental clinics, schools, women's clubs, medical colleges, trade press, daily press). Example: competing toothpaste makers using dental clinics, schools, and the press to explain realistic toothpaste capabilities so honestly advertised products reach their real market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda to combat unethical or unfair advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is potent in meeting unethical or unfair advertising; ethical members of an industry should use propaganda to bring out the basic truths of the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When competitors use exaggerated advertising that undermines an industry, organized truthful propaganda—targeted educational efforts and authoritative channels—can restore public confidence. Example: toothpaste industry response to exaggerated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a wide variety of media and channels
rubrics_metrics.description: News reaches the public through the printed word, pictures, and the ear—books, magazines, letters, posters, banners, newspapers; photographs and motion pictures; lectures, speeches, band music, radio, campaign songs—and all these must be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate tasks to different media according to what each can do best; use printed materials, photographs, motion pictures, radio, speeches, exhibitions, contests, institutes, cooperation with educational institutions, etc. Avoid relying on a single medium ('don't put all one's eggs into one basket').

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific analysis and segmentation of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: To aid in preparation there should be made as nearly scientific an analysis as possible of the public and of the needs of the public; a survey of public desires and demands would come to the aid of the political strategist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct market-style research and surveys before crafting messages; identify which sections are already persuaded to avoid wasted effort; use segmentation to target resources and tailor appeals to specific groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and proportionately allocate campaign funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A political campaign should be budgeted like a business: decide how much to raise, how to raise it, and how money should be spent according to careful and exact budgeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate campaign costs, set fundraising methods (preferably candid/public drives), then allocate funds proportionally across newspapers, periodicals, posters, motion pictures, events, and local activities. Certain expenditures may be warranted only if they are a small part of the budget; large relative expenditures must be justified by their place in the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and candor in fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which money should be raised: politics would gain much in prestige if the money-raising campaign were conducted candidly and publicly, like campaigns for war funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider public and open fundraising models (e.g., charity-drive style) to eliminate secret 'black bag' elements and to increase public trust and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronize all forms of appeal (integrated campaign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is done must be synchronized accurately with all other forms of appeal to the public; one method of appeal is merely one method of appeal and one dare not put all one's eggs into one basket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure timing, message, symbolism, and media placement are coordinated—the radio address, printed materials, public events, and endorsements must reinforce one another rather than act at cross-purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional appeals must be coherent and targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: To appeal to the emotions of the public in a political campaign is indispensable, but the emotional content must (a) coincide in every way with the broad basic plans of the campaign and all its minor details; (b) be adapted to the many groups of the public at which it is to be aimed; and (c) conform to the media of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid haphazard, maudlin, or sentimental stunts. Emotional acts (e.g., kissing babies) are effective only when they symbolize a concrete plank in the platform and are synchronized with the campaign's message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dramatic circumstances to make issues self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: A propagandist uses strategy to dramatize an issue so that the contention becomes dramatic and self-evident rather than merely argued at listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage exhibitions, simultaneous city events, boycotts, or symbolic actions that make abstract claims visible and persuasive (example: staging low-tariff exhibitions in many cities with prominent inaugurations). Use dramatization to reduce reliance on pure argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble authoritative endorsers and opinion leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together groups with authority—society leaders, style experts, fashion editors, artists, and distinguished committees—to give credibility and visibility to an appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit respected authorities and organize events (e.g., fashion fêtes, testimonial days) so their names and presence authenticate the message. Example: millinery industry used a committee of artists and fashion editors to restore large hats to vogue; Beech-Nut used a hometown testimonial to rebut sale rumors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle crises and false rumors promptly and effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the public relations counsel is called in to handle an emergency situation; a false rumor may occasion an enormous loss in prestige and money if not handled promptly and effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid, authoritative clarification is essential; sometimes symbolic community actions (e.g., public testimonials) are more convincing than denials. Examples: Hudson Motor Co. false dividend report and the Beech-Nut hometown testimonial that disproved sale rumors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep continuous 'finger on the public pulse' and adapt
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern business must have its finger continuously on the public pulse. It must understand the changes in the public mind and be prepared to interpret itself fairly and eloquently to changing opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor public knowledge and taste; update messaging, products, and PR tactics to reflect evolving public sentiment. The publicity director must be a businessperson, not a stunt artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize program and capacity over personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the party's program and the candidate's ability to carry it out—'Not personality, but the ability of the candidate to carry out the party’s program adequately, and the program itself should be emphasized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While personality helps sell a platform, avoid substituting charm for substance; align personal appeals to demonstrate capability and policy implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate appeals by group identities, not just party labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is made up of interlocking groups—economic, social, religious, educational, cultural, racial, collegiate, local, sports, and hundreds of others—and campaigns must define the group appeal they will use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map relevant interest groups for the issue (e.g., mothers, physicians, educators for maternal-health legislation) and design targeted appeals and mobilization strategies for those groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train or recruit professional propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians should be trained as propagandists; bright young men might be apprenticed to professional propagandists before serving the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring PR professionals into campaign teams or train campaign staff in modern mass-distribution techniques rather than relying on antiquated political methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit small distinguishing features to create perceived value
rubrics_metrics.description: A minor element can be made to assume economic importance by being established in the public mind as a matter of style (e.g., paint typewriters in cheerful hues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social psychology principles (gregariousness, obedience to authority, emulation) to convert small product differences into style-based consumer preferences, thereby avoiding destructive price-only competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use association and cooperative efforts against inter-commodity competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-commodity competition cannot be fought single-handed; businesses increasingly call upon their trade associations to help because cooperative advertising and association efforts counteract competing product groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize cooperative advertising and trade-association initiatives to present unified responses against competing product categories that steal market share (examples discussed: food producers, building materials).
